title: Unique Paths
description: Count paths from top-left to bottom-right in an m×n grid moving only right or down. Classic 2D DP: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1], with the entire first row and first column equal to 1.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm given an `m × n` grid. I start at the top-left cell `(0, 0)` and want to reach the bottom-right cell `(m-1, n-1)`. At each step I can move only RIGHT or DOWN — no diagonals, no backtracking. How many distinct paths get me there?"

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Are obstacles in the grid possible? (If yes, that's Unique Paths II, slightly different.)
• What if `m` or `n` is 1 — single row or column? Just one path?
• What are the bounds on `m` and `n`? (Affects whether `O(m·n)` is acceptable, and whether the answer overflows JS Numbers.)
• Return value — just the count, or also the actual paths?
sections.why: The obstacle question is the big one — Unique Paths and Unique Paths II share the recurrence shape but Paths II adds a 'if cell is blocked, dp[i][j] = 0' branch. Confirming no obstacles keeps this the clean Pascal's-triangle version. The bounds question matters because `C(m+n-2, m-1)` (the closed-form answer) gets large fast — at `m=n=20`, the answer is already around `10^11`, well past `2^32`.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious exponential solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is recursive: `paths(i, j) = paths(i+1, j) + paths(i, j+1)`, with base case `paths(m-1, n-1) = 1` (reached the end — one path: the empty path of zero moves) and out-of-bounds returning 0. That's `O(2^(m+n))` time because at every cell you branch in two directions and recurse `m+n-2` deep total. Same `2^k` blow-up as the recursive Fibonacci, and the overlap is enormous — `paths(2, 3)` gets computed from many `(i, j)` ancestors. Memoization on `(i, j)` brings it to `O(m·n)` time."
sections.why: Naming the recursive 'go right or go down' shape is what plants the recurrence — and it makes the bottom-up table feel like a translation rather than a discovery. The exponential overlap is the justification for DP; once that's established, the rest (memo → bottom-up → space optimization) is mechanical.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to 2D bottom-up tabulation?
sections.say:
"This is classic 2D grid DP. The recurrence: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]` — the number of paths to cell `(i, j)` equals the number that came from above (the last move was DOWN) plus the number that came from the left (the last move was RIGHT). Those are the only two ways to enter the cell, and they don't overlap (different last moves), so addition is correct.

The base case lives entirely on the top row and left column: there's exactly one path to any cell on the top edge (all RIGHTs) and exactly one path to any cell on the left edge (all DOWNs). The cleanest way to encode that is to initialize the whole grid to 1 — that pre-fills row 0 and column 0 in one shot — then only iterate the interior cells starting at `(1, 1)`.

Answer at `dp[m-1][n-1]`. Time `O(m·n)`, space `O(m·n)` (can drop to `O(n)` with rolling row)."
sections.why: Articulating the recurrence as 'last move was DOWN or RIGHT, sum the two predecessors' is the load-bearing pedagogy — it gives the same 'decision at each step' framing as the 1D DPs, just in 2D. The 'init all-1s pre-fills the base case' trick is a small but elegant detail; saying it out loud signals you've thought about how to make the init code minimal rather than writing two separate base-case loops.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — the small symmetric case, a slightly wider rectangle, and the medium square that confirms Pascal's-triangle growth.

examples.note: Symmetric small case — by symmetry of the binomial coefficient, m=3 n=3 gives C(4,2)=6.
Asymmetric rectangle — C(5,2) = 10. The grid produces Pascal-triangle values along its diagonals.
Medium square — C(6,3) = 20. Confirms the binomial formula matches the DP.

sections.why: Tracing surfaces three things. (1) The grid IS Pascal's triangle rotated 45 degrees — each cell is `C(i+j, i)` — which is the closed-form solution if you want `O(m+n)` time with no DP at all. Naming that out loud shows you see the combinatorial structure. (2) The 'init all-1s' trick is what makes the DP code clean — if you forgot it and had to write `if (i === 0 || j === 0) dp[i][j] = 1`, the loop body gets cluttered. (3) The asymmetric case validates that the loop bounds (`i < m`, `j < n`) work for non-square grids without modification.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• `m = 1` or `n = 1` — a single row or column. The all-1s init covers it; the interior loop never runs because `i < m` (or `j < n`) is immediately false. Returns dp[0][n-1] = 1 (one path: all RIGHTs).
• `m = 1, n = 1` — start equals end. One path: the empty path. dp[0][0] = 1. ✓
• Very large `m` and `n` — say `m = n = 30`. The answer is `C(58, 29) ≈ 3 × 10^16`, which is just past JS's safe integer limit (`2^53 ≈ 9 × 10^15`). For `m + n > 60` you risk precision loss; switch to BigInt if exact arithmetic matters.
• Asymmetric extremes — `m = 100, n = 2`. Only 100 paths (you pick where the single RIGHT goes, the rest are DOWNs). The DP handles it; runtime is tiny.
• Obstacles in the grid (Unique Paths II variant) — not in this spec, but worth flagging: if grid[i][j] is blocked, force dp[i][j] = 0 and the propagation skips it naturally. Same `O(m·n)` time.
• Closed-form alternative — `C(m+n-2, m-1)` computes the answer in `O(min(m, n))` time with no DP at all. Faster but harder to extend (e.g. Paths II can't use the closed form)."
sections.why: Flagging the safe-integer-precision boundary at `m + n > 60` is the senior signal — most candidates don't even notice that the DP can silently lose precision past `2^53`. Mentioning the closed-form `C(m+n-2, m-1)` shows you see the combinatorial structure (which the trace section also surfaced); the interviewer either nods or pushes back with 'what if obstacles are added?', at which point you have the DP variant ready.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is `O(m·n)` — `m·n` cells, constant work per cell (one add, one assignment). Space is `O(m·n)` for the dp table.

The naive recursive version was `O(2^(m+n))`; memoization brings it to `O(m·n)`; bottom-up keeps the same bounds with smaller constants (no recursion overhead).

Space optimization: each cell only reads the cell above (previous row, same column) and the cell to the left (current row, previous column). So a single row of length `n` suffices — process left to right, the value at `newRow[j]` after updating becomes the new 'above' for the next row, and `newRow[j-1]` is the 'left'. Drops space to `O(n)` (or `O(min(m, n))` by orienting the loop on the smaller dimension).

Closed-form alternative: the answer is `C(m+n-2, m-1)` (choose which `m-1` of the total `m+n-2` moves are DOWNs). Computable in `O(min(m, n))` time with one combinatorial loop and no DP. Faster, but loses the ability to handle obstacles or per-cell weights.

Template variants: Unique Paths II (add obstacles — same DP with a zero-out for blocked cells); Minimum Path Sum (change `+` to `min` and accumulate cell values — same 2D shape); Maximum Path Sum and Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix (more complex but share the 'every cell depends on neighbors' structure)."
sections.why: Walking the `2^(m+n) → m·n → n` space progression is the standard defense. Naming the `O(min(m, n))` closed-form alternative AND its limitation (no obstacles, no per-cell weights) is the senior signal — most candidates either don't know the closed form, or quote it without flagging when it breaks. The Minimum Path Sum / Paths II extensions prove you see this as one cell of a template family — grid DP problems all share the 'sum-of-neighbors' or 'min-of-neighbors' shape, and recognizing the family is what makes the next variant trivial.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the m×n grid DP. Init pre-fills every cell with 1 — that handles the top row and left column (single path along any edge). Each interior cell is the sum of the cell above and the cell to its left.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter — grid ${m}x${n}`, state: { m, n } };
const dp = Array.from({ length: m }, () => new Array(n).fill(1));
yield { line: 3, label: `init dp[${m}][${n}] all 1s — pre-fills row 0 and col 0 (single path along any edge)`, state: { m, n, dp: snap() } };
yield { line: 8, label: `dp[${i}][${j}] = top(${top}) + left(${left}) = ${dp[i][j]}`, state: { m, n, i, j, dp: snap(), lastFilled: [i, j] } };
yield { line: 11, label: `return dp[${m - 1}][${n - 1}] = ${dp[m - 1][n - 1]}`, state: { m, n, dp: snap(), returns: dp[m - 1][n - 1] } };

reference.approach: 2D grid DP — paths in from above plus paths in from the left
notes: First row and first column are all 1 — there is exactly one way to reach any cell on the top edge (all rights) or the left edge (all downs).
Recurrence dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] says: paths to (i,j) = paths through the cell above + paths through the cell to the left.
Space can drop to O(n) by reusing a single row left-to-right (newRow[j] += newRow[j-1]).
reference.crux: You enter a cell from above (last move DOWN) or the left (last move RIGHT), so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]; the top row and left column are all 1.
cruxDistractors: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) + 1 — that finds a longest path length, not the COUNT of distinct paths.
Greedily move toward the corner with more remaining cells at each step and count one path — there is exactly one greedy walk, ignoring the combinatorial branching.
Multiply the two predecessors: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] · dp[i][j-1], treating the entry directions as independent choices to combine.

alternates.label: Rolling row (O(n) space)
alternates.when: Reach for this when an interviewer asks 'can you reduce space?' after seeing the 2D table. Each cell only reads the cell directly above (previous row, same column) and the cell to its left (same row). One row of length n is enough — update it in-place left-to-right.
notes: row[j] before the update is dp[i-1][j] (the cell above); row[j-1] after update is dp[i][j-1] (the cell to the left) — one array covers both.
The left column implicitly stays 1 because j starts at 1 and row[0] is never modified (it's always the base-case 1).
For a further O(min(m,n)) variant, swap m and n so the shorter dimension is the column — the row array is then length min(m,n).

alternates.label: Combinatorics: C(m+n-2, m-1) (O(min(m,n)) time)
alternates.when: Reach for this when you recognize the combinatorial structure: every path from (0,0) to (m-1,n-1) is a sequence of exactly (m-1) DOWNs and (n-1) RIGHTs in some order. The answer is just choose which (m-1) of the (m+n-2) moves are DOWNs. This is O(min(m,n)) time and O(1) space — much faster than any DP approach. Skip it if obstacles are possible (Unique Paths II), since the closed form doesn't extend to blocked cells.
notes: C(m+n-2, m-1) counts the number of ways to arrange (m-1) DOWNs and (n-1) RIGHTs — every distinct arrangement is a unique path.
Compute iteratively as result *= (total-i)/(i+1) to stay integer at each step (JS floats handle this exactly for small m,n; switch to BigInt near m+n≈60).
Cannot extend to Unique Paths II (obstacles) or Minimum Path Sum — those require the DP table.

questions.q: What is the recurrence for Unique Paths?
questions.explain: You can only arrive at (i,j) from above or from the left, and those two sets of paths are disjoint, so the counts add. Taking a max would OPTIMISE over paths (the Min/Max Path Sum shape) instead of counting them.

questions.q: Why is the entire first row filled with 1?
options: To match the convention from Pascal's triangle, where the outer rows are bordered with 1 to anchor the recurrence
There is exactly one path along the top edge — all moves are rights
Because dp[0][j] would otherwise be undefined and break the dp[i-1][j] read on row 1
Because the first row represents the cumulative path count after the first move from (0,0) — always exactly one move
questions.explain: On row 0 there is no cell above, so the only legal move is right — one path to every top-edge cell. The same argument fills column 0 with all-downs, which is why `fill(1)` covers both bases and the loops can start at i=1, j=1.

questions.q: Time complexity of the 2D DP solution?
questions.explain: Every one of the m×n cells is written exactly once with a single add. The exponential figure is the un-memoised recursion that re-walks each path; the table is what collapses it.

questions.q: How can you reduce space from O(m*n) to O(n)?
options: Use the closed-form binomial C(m+n-2, m-1) — but that gives O(1) space, not O(n)
Reuse a single row of length n, updating left-to-right
Store only the diagonals of the dp table — there are O(m+n) of them, each O(1) wide on average
Use only `dp[i][j-1]` and skip the row-above lookup — the answer doubles each step so the row-above term is implied
questions.explain: Each cell depends only on the cell above (previous row, same column) and the cell to the left (current row). One row suffices.
